newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blue chips close modestly lower, techs strong.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blue chips close modestly lower, techs strong.

text.p: U.S. blue chip stocks closed with modest losses on Wednesday while technology and small-cap stocks thrived even amid a sell-off in the bond market.

The Dow Jones industrial average dipped 13 points, or 0.17 percent, to close unofficially at 7290 in heavy trading. The Standard & Poor's 500 index also finished lower, down 2.27 at 839.39 unofficially, though both indices had managed to trim earlier losses that came as the price of the long bond slid.

Treasury prices slumped after news that the U.S. trade deficit narrowed 19.3 percent to $8.51 billion in March, well below economists' forecasts, as total exports and imports reached all-time highs. The long bond was off 24/32 to yield 6.96 percent late in the session.

Strong-than-expected trade activity means the government may have to raise its initial estimate of 5.6 percent growth in U.S. gross domestic product in the first quarter, economists said. That view lent credence to the opinion that the Federal Reserve may soon be forced to boost interest rates to slow growth and prevent inflation from accelerating.
Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Nesbitt Burns, said the strength in exports was especially surprising because the dollar had been strong in March, before its recent weakening.
On Wednesday, the dollar achieved modest gains after a steep slide the previous day after Fed policy-makers elected to make no change in interest rates.

Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer for First Albany, said the Treasury market also suffered because of concern that a falling U.S. currency might encourage foreign investors to switch out of dollar-denominated bonds.
But the declines in the bond market did nothing to slow technology and small-capitalization stocks, as both the Nasdaq Composite and the Russell 2000 finished in positive territory.

Dell Computer Corp led a rally in personal computer stocks after the company reported first-quarter earnings that easily beat forecasts. The report, released after the market's close on Tuesday, was interpreted as a signal of strong PC demand.
Dell jumped 7-1/8 in heavy trading to close at 106-3/4, after reaching fresh high of 109-3/4. The company also set a two-for-one stock split.

PC makers Compaq Computer Corp, up 5-3/4 at 102-3/4, and Gateway 2000 Inc also hit 52-week highs, though Gateway later retreated after unveiling a low-cost network PC. The stock closed down 1-7/8 to 69-1/4.

Computer networking stocks also shone as momentum investors moved back into the sector, traders said. 3Com rose 2-5/8 to 41-5/8, Cisco Systems Inc gained 1-3/8 to 65-3/4, and Ascend Communications Inc rose 1-1/2 to 51-1/2.
The Nasdaq Composite closed up 9.87, or 0.72 percent, to 1373.75. The Russell 2000 added 1.86 to 370.06.
"With a backup in long-term interest rates, at a time when the market is arguably overvalued, one of the only places portfolio managers feel comfortable is in smaller stocks," Johnson said.
He said the valuations of many large-cap stocks may be too high for those concerned about the impact of rising rates on earnings growth.

Keystone International Inc rose more than 55 percent to close up 10-5/8 to 31-1/8. Before the opening, Tyco International Inc said it would buy Keystone for $1.2 billion in stock. Tyco lost 1-1/8 to close at 61-5/8.
Harnischfeger Industries fell 3-3/8 to 38-5/8 after it warned that earnings in its current fiscal year could fall short of forecasts because of softness in its mining-equipment business.

Tobacco shares rallied. Philip Morris Cos Inc, UST Inc and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp gained after an analyst said he expected a deal to settle litigation pending against the industry within three weeks.

The gains came before a late-afternoon announcement that a Maryland court ruled that the state did not have a right to recover from tobacco companies Medicaid payments made on behalf of individual smokers.
About 540 million shares were traded on the New York Stock Exchange. Advancing stocks outnumbered decliners 1420 to 1108.
The S&P 500 fell 2.31 to 839.35.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1881))
